title: 嘉靖十九年廣東鄉試錄
text:
第壹場
四書
君子無終食之間違仁造次必於是顛沛
必於是
蕭來鳳
同考試官教諭蕭批造次顛沛時功夫極難更詳之
考試官教諭劉批能體認
考試官教授林批明浄
君子體仁之功隨所寓而見其密焉夫仁者君
===
===
子所以成德者也體之於身而不以所寓遷焉
則其存養者不已密乎夫子之意以為君子審
擇於富貴貧賤而不苟者凡以求仁也仁其可
已乎哉是故終食者富貴貧賤之小者也君子
則自其不處不去者而精之時乎當取固致謹
矣而其為仁之心不以時取而始存時乎當舍
固致决矣而其克己之念不以時舍而始有蓋
其天德完備合大小以為功至理渾全貫心事
而成體曷嘗少離於一飯之頃乎至若造次而
punctuated:
第壹場
四書
「君子無終食之間違仁，造次必於是，顛沛必於是。」
蕭來鳳
同考試官教諭蕭批：「造次顛沛時功夫極難，更詳之。」
考試官教諭劉批：「能體認。」
考試官教授林批：「明浄。」
君子體仁之功，隨所寓而見其密焉。夫仁者，君子所以成德者也。體之於身，而不以所寓遷焉，則其存養者不已密乎？夫子之意，以為君子審擇於富貴貧賤而不苟者，凡以求仁也。仁其可已乎哉？是故終食者，富貴貧賤之小者也。君子則自其不處不去者而精之。時乎當取，固致謹矣，而其為仁之心，不以時取而始存；時乎當舍，固致决矣，而其克己之念，不以時舍而始有。蓋其天德完備，合大小以為功；至理渾全，貫心事而成體。曷嘗少離於一飯之頃乎？至若造次而
translation_en:
First Session
Four Books
“The gentleman does not depart from benevolence even for the time it takes to finish a meal. In moments of haste he invariably abides in it; in adversity he invariably abides in it.”
Xiao Laifeng
Associate Examiner Xiao, Instructor, comments: “The work of cultivation in moments of haste and adversity is exceedingly difficult. Elaborate further on this.”
Examiner Liu, Instructor, comments: “Shows an ability to apprehend its meaning personally.”
Examiner Lin, Professor, comments: “Clear and clean.”
The thoroughness of the gentleman’s work of embodying benevolence reveals itself in whatever circumstances he encounters. Benevolence is that by which the gentleman perfects his virtue. If he embodies it in his person without changing according to his circumstances, is his work of preserving and nurturing it not already thorough? The Master’s meaning is that the gentleman carefully judges his choices concerning wealth and rank, poverty and low station, and does nothing heedlessly, solely in order to seek benevolence. How could the practice of benevolence ever cease?
Thus, the time taken to finish a meal is a lesser instance of the circumstances of wealth and rank, poverty and low station. The gentleman refines still further the practice by which he neither remains in improperly obtained wealth and rank nor abandons poverty and low station. When it is time to accept, he certainly exercises the utmost care; yet his resolve to practice benevolence does not first arise only when the time comes to accept. When it is time to relinquish, he certainly acts with the utmost resolution; yet his intent to master himself does not first exist only when the time comes to relinquish. For his Heaven-endowed virtue is complete, and his cultivation embraces great and small alike; the supreme principle is an integral whole, uniting mind and affairs in a single embodiment. How could he ever depart from benevolence even briefly during the span of a meal? As for moments of haste, when …

title: 嘉靖十九年廣東鄉試錄
text:
爲急遽苟且之時則其時爲又近人之所易忽
者也君子則本體自然不容人力造次之心即
其終食之心終食之心行於造次而不與焉固
無有惑之者自夫時而論之斯謂之造次云耳
顛沛而爲傾覆流離之際則其遇爲尤逆人之
所易動者也君子則本體固有不待人爲顛沛
之心即其平居之心平居之心行於顛沛而不
與焉固無有變之者自夫遇而觀之殆謂之顛
沛云耳所以然者仁本無物故不可以有物戕
===
若見物而后覺焉則其於仁也遠矣功在事先
故不可以有事勝若臨事而后養焉則其於造
次顛沛也離矣此君子存養之功所以爲密而
不處不去之迹不足言也雖然不處不去固所
以爲仁矣然以原憲之貧子路之不耻與狐貉
者立而夫子不與其仁何也二子者未見夫仁
之體是以雖有所得猶不免於意必之心而未
大耳此夫子言取舍之分而必繼之以仁者以
此故曰見大則心泰心泰則無不足通於此者
punctuated: 爲急遽苟且之時，則其時爲又近，人之所易忽者也。君子則本體自然，不容人力；造次之心，即其終食之心。終食之心行於造次而不與焉，固無有惑之者。自夫時而論之，斯謂之造次云耳。顛沛而爲傾覆流離之際，則其遇爲尤逆，人之所易動者也。君子則本體固有，不待人爲；顛沛之心，即其平居之心。平居之心行於顛沛而不與焉，固無有變之者。自夫遇而觀之，殆謂之顛沛云耳。所以然者，仁本無物，故不可以有物戕；若見物而后覺焉，則其於仁也遠矣。功在事先，故不可以有事勝；若臨事而后養焉，則其於造次顛沛也離矣。此君子存養之功所以爲密，而不處不去之迹不足言也。雖然，不處不去固所以爲仁矣，然以原憲之貧、子路之不耻與狐貉者立，而夫子不與其仁，何也？二子者未見夫仁之體，是以雖有所得，猶不免於意必之心，而未大耳。此夫子言取舍之分，而必繼之以仁者，以此。故曰：「見大則心泰，心泰則無不足。」通於此者，
translation_en:
…being a time of haste and makeshift action, the moment is still more immediate [?], and thus one in which people easily become heedless. For the gentleman, however, the fundamental substance of his moral nature is spontaneously so, admitting no human contrivance. His mind in moments of haste is the very mind he maintains throughout a meal. That mind operates amid haste without becoming implicated in it; nothing can bewilder it. Only in terms of the circumstances of the moment do we call this “haste.” When adversity brings ruin and displacement, the circumstances encountered are especially unfavorable and readily unsettle people. For the gentleman, however, the fundamental substance is inherently present and does not depend on human contrivance. His mind in adversity is the very mind he has in ordinary life. That mind operates amid adversity without becoming implicated in it; nothing can alter it. Only from the standpoint of the circumstances encountered do we call this “adversity.”

The reason is that benevolence is originally free of external things and therefore cannot be injured by them. If one becomes aware only after encountering things, one is far from benevolence. The work of cultivation precedes affairs, and therefore affairs cannot overwhelm it. If one begins nurturing the mind only when affairs arise, one departs from benevolence in haste and adversity. This is why the gentleman’s work of preserving and nurturing his moral nature is so thorough, while the outward traces of his refusing to remain in improperly acquired wealth and rank or to escape improperly from poverty and low station scarcely merit discussion.

Nevertheless, refusing to remain or to depart is indeed a means of practicing benevolence. Yet despite Yuan Xian’s poverty and Zilu’s feeling no shame at standing beside those wearing fox and badger furs, the Master did not accord them the designation of benevolent. Why? These two had not perceived the substance of benevolence. Thus, although they had attained something, they remained subject to a mind given to preconceptions and insistence, and had yet to attain breadth. This is why, when the Master speaks of the distinction between accepting and rejecting, he invariably follows it with benevolence. Hence the saying: “When one perceives what is great, the mind is at ease; when the mind is at ease, nothing is lacking.” As for one who comprehends this…

title: 嘉靖十九年廣東鄉試錄
text:
顏氏之子其殆庶幾乎
温故而知新敦厚以崇禮
高士楠
同考試官教諭王批〔知新崇禮處似能見得〕
同考試官教諭劉批〔功夫説歸知能上端有着落〕
同考試官教諭徐批〔簡潔〕
考試官教諭劉批〔中庸義當如此作〕
考試官教授林批〔典實可取〕
中庸論體道知能之功各相因而至焉夫知能
===
者包小大而渾焉者也中庸互因其功言之而
體道之全德見矣意謂君子之學固在致極以
弘其大盡道以會其微然要其用功之實豈有
他哉求諸吾心之知能焉得之矣是故吾心固
有之知不假外求者所謂故也故非以强索見
也君子則涵泳以温之既不敢忘以昧其恒覺
之性亦不敢助以害其自然之眞吾順吾事惟
欲養其所有而已然非有知新之益固有之故
豈如是哉又必有温則有知成心忘而端倪見
punctuated:
顏氏之子，其殆庶幾乎！

温故而知新，敦厚以崇禮。
高士楠
同考試官教諭王批〔知新崇禮處似能見得〕
同考試官教諭劉批〔功夫説歸知能上端有着落〕
同考試官教諭徐批〔簡潔〕
考試官教諭劉批〔中庸義當如此作〕
考試官教授林批〔典實可取〕

《中庸》論體道，知能之功各相因而至焉。夫知能者，包小大而渾焉者也。《中庸》互因其功言之，而體道之全德見矣。意謂君子之學，固在致極以弘其大，盡道以會其微。然要其用功之實，豈有他哉？求諸吾心之知能焉，得之矣。是故吾心固有之知，不假外求者，所謂故也。故非以强索見也，君子則涵泳以温之。既不敢忘以昧其恒覺之性，亦不敢助以害其自然之眞。吾順吾事，惟欲養其所有而已。然非有知新之益，固有之故豈如是哉？又必有温則有知，成心忘而端倪見，
translation_en:
…the son of the Yan family must surely have come close!

“Review what is old and thereby understand what is new; deepen one's substantial goodness and thereby honor ritual propriety.”
Gao Shinan

Associate Examiner Wang, an Instructor, comments: 〔The passages on understanding what is new and honoring ritual propriety seem to show genuine insight.〕
Associate Examiner Liu, an Instructor, comments: 〔By bringing the discussion of self-cultivation back to knowing and acting, the essay gives it a definite grounding.〕
Associate Examiner Xu, an Instructor, comments: 〔Concise and lucid.〕
Examiner Liu, an Instructor, comments: 〔This is how an essay on the meaning of the Doctrine of the Mean should be written.〕
Examiner Lin, a Professor, comments: 〔Sound and substantial; worthy of acceptance.〕

In discussing the embodiment of the Way, the Doctrine of the Mean explains how the work of knowing and of acting each builds upon what precedes it and thus reaches fulfillment. Knowing and acting encompass both the small and the great in a unified whole. The Doctrine of the Mean discusses the successive, connected stages of this work, thereby revealing the complete virtue of embodying the Way. Its meaning is that the gentleman's learning certainly consists in reaching the utmost to extend its greatness and fully realizing the Way to comprehend its subtleties. Yet, as for the essential substance of his efforts, could it lie anywhere else? By seeking it in his own mind's capacity to know and act, he finds it.

Thus, the knowledge inherent in my mind, which requires no outward seeking, is what is called “the old.” This old knowledge is not revealed through forced searching; the gentleman immerses himself in it and reflects upon it, thereby reviewing it. He dares neither to forget it, obscuring his nature's constant awareness, nor to force its growth, harming its natural authenticity. I follow the proper course in my affairs, desiring only to nourish what I already possess. Yet without the benefit of understanding what is new, how could this inherent old knowledge attain such a state? Moreover, review must give rise to understanding: fixed preconceptions are forgotten, and the first intimations become apparent…

title: 嘉靖十九年廣東鄉試錄
text:
習見息而生意滋即於吾之所謂故者而益日
新焉以擴充其本體之明温故也知新也一天
性之生生而不可已者也其不兼致矣乎至若
吾心固有之能不待外益者所謂厚也厚非以
掩襲得也君子則篤行以敦之主之以忠信而
不可拔守之以質直而不敢漓吾厚吾生惟欲
立其所有而已然非有崇禮之實固有之能豈
如是哉又必曰敦則日崇忠信之存而制義已
精質直之中而品節惟密即於吾之所謂厚者
===
而益日謹焉以克復其本體之誠敦厚也崇禮
也一天德之成能而不可二者也不其並進矣
乎此知能之功所以相因而尊德問學者有所
不能外也雖然子思之言之詳也非以多言悔
道也為夫學之偏者言之也學之有偏於外者
故曰温故曰敦厚而亦有偏於內者故曰知新
曰崇禮並言之而后中者立矣猶之存心致知
之說博約精一之說也不得其說而徒為內外
之辨則子思之意遠矣是故子思之所憂也
punctuated:
習見息而生意滋，即於吾之所謂故者而益日新焉，以擴充其本體之明。温故也，知新也，一天性之生生而不可已者也，其不兼致矣乎？至若吾心固有之能，不待外益者，所謂厚也。厚非以掩襲得也，君子則篤行以敦之，主之以忠信而不可拔，守之以質直而不敢漓。吾厚吾生，惟欲立其所有而已。然非有崇禮之實，固有之能豈如是哉？又必曰敦則日崇，忠信之存而制義已精，質直之中而品節惟密，即於吾之所謂厚者而益日謹焉，以克復其本體之誠。敦厚也，崇禮也，一天德之成能而不可二者也，不其並進矣乎？此知能之功所以相因，而尊德問學者有所不能外也。

雖然，子思之言之詳也，非以多言悔道也，為夫學之偏者言之也。學之有偏於外者，故曰温故，曰敦厚；而亦有偏於內者，故曰知新，曰崇禮。並言之而后中者立矣。猶之存心致知之說、博約精一之說也。不得其說而徒為內外之辨，則子思之意遠矣。是故子思之所憂也。
translation_en:
…habitual ways of seeing subside and the impulse toward life flourishes. Within what I call the old, there is thus daily renewal, expanding the illumination inherent in the mind’s original substance. Reviewing the old and knowing the new are the ceaseless generation and regeneration of a single Heaven-endowed nature. Must they not both be brought to fulfillment? As for the capacity inherent in my mind, which requires no addition from outside, this is what is called substantiality. Substantiality cannot be acquired through imitation. The gentleman strengthens it through earnest practice, grounding it in loyalty and trustworthiness so that it cannot be uprooted, and maintaining it through simplicity and uprightness, never daring to let it become diluted. In giving substance to my life, I seek only to establish what it already possesses. Yet without the actual practice of honoring ritual propriety, how could this inherent capacity become such? It must also be said that daily strengthening brings daily elevation: with loyalty and trustworthiness preserved, the determination of what is right becomes refined; amid simplicity and uprightness, distinctions and regulations become exact. Within what I call substantiality, one thus becomes more circumspect each day, restoring the sincerity of the mind’s original substance. Strengthening substantiality and honoring ritual propriety are the perfected capacities of a single Heavenly virtue and cannot be treated as two. Must they not advance together? This is why the work of developing knowledge and capacity is mutually dependent, and why those who honor their virtuous nature and pursue inquiry and learning cannot depart from it.

Nevertheless, Zisi’s detailed exposition was not intended to ‘bring regret upon the Way through excessive words’ [?]; he spoke for those whose learning was one-sided. Because some learners lean toward the external, he speaks of reviewing the old and strengthening substantiality; because others lean toward the internal, he speaks of knowing the new and honoring ritual propriety. Only when both are stated together is the mean established. This is like the teachings on preserving the mind and extending knowledge, on breadth of learning and restraint, and on refinement and single-mindedness. If one fails to grasp these teachings and merely argues over the internal and the external, one strays far from Zisi’s intention. This, therefore, is what concerned Zisi.

title: 嘉靖十九年廣東鄉試錄
text:
聖人既竭目力焉繼之以規矩準繩以為
方員平直不可勝用也既竭耳力焉繼
之以六律正五音不可勝用也既竭心
思焉繼之以不忍人之政而仁覆天下
矣
譚維鼎
考試官教諭劉批〔得孟子言心法之意〕
考試官教授林批〔不冗錄出〕
大賢廣聖人心法之用以見其可因也蓋法者
===
心之著也聖人用之以盡民利為政者其亦知
所因哉孟子意謂為政之道非心不立非法不
行法之善者雖聖人莫違焉聖人欲制器以利
天下嘗竭目力以用吾明矣又即其明者繼之
以規矩準繩焉則軌物飭材制器之法立而後
天下之為方員平直者以物付物以與之無窮
而聖人目力之所不及者固在也欲作樂以和
天下嘗竭耳力以用吾聰矣又即其聰者繼之
以六律焉則稽數考聲作樂之法立而後天□
punctuated:
聖人既竭目力焉，繼之以規矩準繩，以為方員平直，不可勝用也；既竭耳力焉，繼之以六律，正五音，不可勝用也；既竭心思焉，繼之以不忍人之政，而仁覆天下矣。
譚維鼎。
考試官教諭劉批〔得孟子言心法之意〕
考試官教授林批〔不冗，錄出〕
大賢廣聖人心法之用，以見其可因也。蓋法者，心之著也。聖人用之以盡民利，為政者其亦知所因哉！孟子意謂，為政之道，非心不立，非法不行。法之善者，雖聖人莫違焉。聖人欲制器以利天下，嘗竭目力以用吾明矣；又即其明者，繼之以規矩準繩焉，則軌物飭材、制器之法立，而後天下之為方員平直者，以物付物，以與之無窮，而聖人目力之所不及者固在也。欲作樂以和天下，嘗竭耳力以用吾聰矣；又即其聰者，繼之以六律焉，則稽數考聲、作樂之法立，而後天□
translation_en:
“Having exhausted the powers of their eyes, the sages supplemented them with compasses, squares, levels, and marking cords, to produce squares, circles, level surfaces, and straight lines, whose uses are inexhaustible. Having exhausted the powers of their ears, they supplemented them with the six pitch standards to regulate the five notes, whose uses are inexhaustible. Having exhausted their powers of thought, they supplemented them with government that could not bear to see others suffer, and benevolence thus extended over all under Heaven.”
Tan Weiding.
Comment by Examiner Liu, an Instructor: 〔Grasps what Mencius meant in speaking of the mind and its methods.〕
Comment by Examiner Lin, a Professor: 〔Not prolix; selected for inclusion.〕
The great worthy elaborates upon the application of the sages’ mind and methods to show that these can be followed. Methods are the manifestation of the mind. The sages employed them to bring the fullest benefit to the people; should those who govern not also know what to follow? Mencius means that the way of governing cannot be established without the mind and cannot be put into practice without methods. When methods are good, even the sages do not depart from them. Wishing to fashion implements to benefit all under Heaven, the sages exhausted the powers of their eyes to employ their clear sight. They then supplemented that clear sight with compasses, squares, levels, and marking cords. Thus were established methods for giving things their proper form, preparing materials, and fashioning implements. Thereafter, those throughout the world who made squares, circles, level surfaces, and straight lines could apply one physical thing to another, extending these methods without end. There were indeed things beyond the reach of the sages’ own eyesight. Wishing to create music to bring harmony to all under Heaven, they exhausted the powers of their ears to employ their keen hearing. They then supplemented that keen hearing with the six pitch standards. Thus were established methods for examining numerical relationships, investigating sounds, and creating music. Thereafter, throughout Heaven [?] …

title: 嘉靖十九年廣東鄉試錄
text:
之正五音者以數因數以與之無窮而聖人耳
力之所不及者固在也制作且然而況於治乎
夫不忍斯民之陷溺竭心思以圖平治者聖人
之心也心不可見故又制爲教養之政以見之
心以善政政以繼心則仁之道顯而爲治之法
立其諸治之規矩六律矣天下後世用之以感
人心平其政者仁其寧有窮哉仁之無窮卽心
思之無窮也已由是觀之爲政不可以無法欲
立法者必於先王是因也先王之法固吾心之
===
所存者耳雖然孟子之欲人法先王也非以其
迹也以是心而充之也故曰苟能充之足以保
四海齊王之以羊易牛豈無是心者哉要之不
可以王天下未繼其充之之功故耳充之固所
以爲法也若曰心法二用其不流而霸者幾希
易
臨剛浸而長說而順剛中而應大亨以正
天之道也
梁式
punctuated:
之正五音者，以數因數，以與之無窮，而聖人耳力之所不及者固在也。制作且然，而況於治乎？夫不忍斯民之陷溺，竭心思以圖平治者，聖人之心也。心不可見，故又制爲教養之政以見之。心以善政，政以繼心，則仁之道顯，而爲治之法立，其諸治之規矩六律矣！天下後世用之以感人心、平其政者，仁其寧有窮哉？仁之無窮，卽心思之無窮也已。由是觀之，爲政不可以無法，欲立法者，必於先王是因也。先王之法，固吾心之所存者耳。雖然，孟子之欲人法先王也，非以其迹也，以是心而充之也。故曰：「苟能充之，足以保四海。」齊王之以羊易牛，豈無是心者哉？要之，不可以王天下，未繼其充之之功故耳。充之固所以爲法也。若曰心法二用，其不流而霸者幾希！

易

臨，剛浸而長，說而順，剛中而應，大亨以正，天之道也。

梁式
translation_en:
…those who tune the five notes proceed from one numerical relation to another, applying them without end; yet there remain things beyond the reach of the sage’s own hearing. If this is true even of making objects and composing music, how much more so of governing? Unable to bear seeing the people sink into misery, the sage exhausts his thought in seeking peace and good order: such is his heart. Since the heart cannot be seen, he establishes policies for educating and nourishing the people through which to make it manifest. The heart makes government good, and government carries forward the heart’s intentions. Thus the Way of benevolence becomes manifest and standards for government are established. These are surely the compass, square, and six pitch standards of government! When people throughout the world and in later generations use them to move human hearts and bring order to their government, how could benevolence ever be exhausted? The inexhaustibility of benevolence is precisely the inexhaustibility of the heart’s deliberations. Viewed in this light, government cannot dispense with standards, and those wishing to establish standards must take the former kings as their basis. The standards of the former kings are indeed simply what is already present in our own hearts.

Nevertheless, when Mengzi urges people to model themselves on the former kings, he does not mean following their outward deeds, but taking this heart and extending it fully. Thus he says: “If one can fully extend it, it is sufficient to protect all within the Four Seas.” When the king of Qi exchanged an ox for a sheep, was he someone lacking this heart? Ultimately, his inability to rule the world as a true king arose only from his failure to follow through with the work of fully extending it. Fully extending it is precisely how standards are established. If one claims that the heart and standards have separate functions, there is little chance of avoiding a descent into hegemonic rule!

Book of Changes

“Approach: the firm gradually advances and grows; joyful and compliant; the firm occupies the central position and finds a response. Great success through correctness: this is the Way of Heaven.”

Liang Shi

title: 嘉靖十九年廣東鄉試錄
text:
同考試官教諭王批發明剛長臨陰之義殆盡
同考試官教諭劉批講天人處足知學易之功
同考試官教諭徐批歸在人事上最是
考試官教諭劉批理明詞徹
考試官教授林批峻整
彖傳釋卦名見陽長之機必本諸卦而表其占
之善也夫二陽浸長陽道可行之機也况卦具
臨陰之善占之大亨以正者非天理之當然者
乎昔彖傳之意若謂君子小人消長之不一者
===
勢也盡人謀而聽天命者理也茲卦之名為臨
者以卦體言之二陽浸長以逼於陰天啓其運
君子有道長之機自此而為泰為壯其勢不可
禦也時逢其適同道有為朋之益自此而為夬
為乾其漸不可遏也此卦之所以為臨也辭曰
元亨利貞者何哉吾有取於卦之德焉兌說而
坤順是其防陰之道素若安閑固不失於干煩
之壯且順理而行所以正已者不疎矣吾有取
於卦之體焉剛中而五應是其制陰之道動中
punctuated:
同考試官教諭王批：發明剛長臨陰之義殆盡。
同考試官教諭劉批：講天人處，足知學易之功。
同考試官教諭徐批：歸在人事上，最是。
考試官教諭劉批：理明詞徹。
考試官教授林批：峻整。
彖傳釋卦名，見陽長之機，必本諸卦而表其占之善也。夫二陽浸長，陽道可行之機也。况卦具臨陰之善，占之大亨以正者，非天理之當然者乎？昔彖傳之意，若謂君子小人消長之不一者，勢也；盡人謀而聽天命者，理也。茲卦之名為臨者，以卦體言之，二陽浸長以逼於陰，天啓其運，君子有道長之機。自此而為泰、為壯，其勢不可禦也。時逢其適，同道有為朋之益，自此而為夬、為乾，其漸不可遏也。此卦之所以為臨也。辭曰「元亨利貞」者，何哉？吾有取於卦之德焉：兌說而坤順，是其防陰之道，素若安閑，固不失於干煩之壯；且順理而行，所以正已者不疎矣。吾有取於卦之體焉：剛中而五應，是其制陰之道，動中
translation_en:
Associate Examiner Wang, Instructor, comments: “The meaning of the firm growing and drawing near to the yielding is elucidated almost exhaustively.”
Associate Examiner Liu, Instructor, comments: “The discussion of Heaven and humanity reveals the accomplishment attained through studying the Book of Changes.”
Associate Examiner Xu, Instructor, comments: “Bringing the argument back to human affairs is particularly apt.”
Examiner Liu, Instructor, comments: “The principles are clear and the language lucid.”
Examiner Lin, Professor, comments: “Rigorous and orderly.”
The Commentary on the Judgments explains the hexagram’s name and reveals the opportunity presented by the growth of yang. It necessarily grounds its explanation in the hexagram itself and brings out the excellence of its prognostication. The gradual growth of the two yang lines presents an opportunity for the way of yang to prevail. Moreover, since the hexagram possesses the virtues needed for drawing near to yin, is not its prognostication of great success through correctness the necessary course of Heaven’s principle? The intention of the Commentary on the Judgments of old seems to be this: the varying decline and growth of gentlemen and petty men belong to the configuration of circumstances; exhausting human deliberation and then submitting to Heaven’s mandate accords with principle.
This hexagram is named Approach (Lin). Speaking of its structure, the two yang lines gradually grow and press upon yin. Heaven opens the course of their advance, and gentlemen have an opportunity for their way to grow. From here the hexagram becomes Peace (Tai) and then Great Strength (Dazhuang); its momentum cannot be resisted. Meeting with the appropriate time, those who share the same way enjoy the benefit of companionship. From here it becomes Breakthrough (Guai) and then the Creative (Qian); its gradual advance cannot be checked. This is why the hexagram is called Approach.
Why does its judgment say, “Supreme success; beneficial to remain correct”? I draw upon the virtues of the hexagram: Dui is joyful and Kun compliant. Thus its way of guarding against yin is ordinarily composed and at ease; it certainly does not lapse into an importunate, troublesome show of strength [?]. Moreover, by acting in accordance with principle, one leaves nothing neglected in the means of rectifying oneself. I also draw upon the hexagram’s structure: the firm line occupies the center, and the fifth line responds to it. Thus its way of restraining yin, in its action, hits upon…

title: 嘉靖十九年廣東鄉試錄
text:
機會固不拂乎時措之宜且朋來無咎所以協
恭者有人矣夫當剛長之時備臨陰之善如此
故大亨者非偶然之故也蓋天者理而已矣理
之所當得天人相成之妙志氣交應之幾君子
安能以襲取哉利貞者非過爲之防也蓋天者
正而已矣理之所當爲天運而人從時起而事
應君子安能以逆天哉由是觀之世道固不能
以不復人謀亦不可以不臧幸乎天而人不繼
焉豈君子所以處道行之會也哉大抵盛衰相
===
推而運生焉安危相倚而機伏焉世道之不能
以常如一日也然圖回之機未始不於和順得
之任智以穿鑿挾權以急功恃勢以資姦其以
弊天下均也是故事未成而幾先泄功未就而
志已驕君子固病其驟也而陋前規以更張任
己意以推行者卒以啓禍亂之原安危治忽之
機君子可鑒矣
夫易廣矣大矣以言乎遠則不禦以言乎
邇則靜而正以言乎天地之間則備矣
punctuated:
機會，固不拂乎時措之宜；且朋來無咎，所以協恭者有人矣。夫當剛長之時，備臨陰之善如此，故大亨者非偶然之故也。蓋天者理而已矣，理之所當得，天人相成之妙，志氣交應之幾，君子安能以襲取哉？利貞者非過爲之防也。蓋天者正而已矣，理之所當爲，天運而人從，時起而事應，君子安能以逆天哉？由是觀之，世道固不能以不復，人謀亦不可以不臧。幸乎天而人不繼焉，豈君子所以處道行之會也哉？大抵盛衰相推而運生焉，安危相倚而機伏焉，世道之不能以常如一日也。然圖回之機，未始不於和順得之。任智以穿鑿，挾權以急功，恃勢以資姦，其以弊天下均也。是故事未成而幾先泄，功未就而志已驕，君子固病其驟也。而陋前規以更張，任己意以推行者，卒以啓禍亂之原。安危治忽之機，君子可鑒矣。

夫易廣矣，大矣！以言乎遠，則不禦；以言乎邇，則靜而正；以言乎天地之間，則備矣。
translation_en:
…the opportune moment, certainly not contravening what is fitting for action at that time. Moreover, “friends come, and there is no blame”: there are others with whom to cooperate in reverent service. When the firm is growing, provision for approaching the yielding is thus thoroughly made. Hence “supreme success” is no chance occurrence. Heaven is simply principle. What principle warrants, the marvel of Heaven and humanity bringing one another to fulfillment, and the subtle workings through which purpose and vital force respond to one another—how could the gentleman seize these by stealth? “It is beneficial to remain correct” is no excessive precaution. Heaven is simply correctness. In doing what principle requires, people follow Heaven’s movement, and affairs respond as the occasion arises. How could the gentleman go against Heaven? Viewed thus, the course of the age must indeed undergo a return, and human planning must also be sound. To enjoy Heaven’s favor without following it up through human effort—could this be how the gentleman conducts himself when the Way has an opportunity to prevail?

Generally, flourishing and decline displace one another, giving rise to changes of fortune; security and danger depend upon one another, with the seeds of change concealed within them. The course of the age cannot remain the same from day to day. Yet opportunities to turn affairs around have always been found through harmony and accord. Relying on cleverness to devise contrivances, wielding power to hasten achievement, and trusting in influence to further wrongdoing are alike in bringing harm to the world. Thus, before an undertaking is accomplished, its incipient workings are already exposed; before success is attained, ambition has already grown arrogant. The gentleman certainly deplores such precipitancy. Those who disparage established precedents and alter them, imposing their own ideas in carrying matters out, ultimately open the source of calamity and disorder. The gentleman may take warning from these turning points between security and danger, order and disorder.

The Changes is broad indeed, and great indeed! Speaking of what is distant, it knows no bounds; speaking of what is near, it is still and correct; speaking of what lies between Heaven and Earth, it encompasses everything.

title: 嘉靖十九年廣東鄉試錄
text:
夫乾其靜也專其動也直是以大生焉
夫坤其靜也翕其動也闢是以廣生焉
高士楠
同考試官教諭王批說易廣大處不易見得
同考試官教諭劉批長題能收拾
同考試官教諭徐批模寫造化深見易理
考試官教諭劉批辭順理足
考試官教授林批純雅
大傳詳易理之廣大必推而本諸乾坤焉夫易
===
冒天下之道者也乾坤動靜之間而廣大見之
易其性命之書矣乎大傳之意若謂易者理之
會也乾坤者理之迹也人以易爲卜筮之書非
知易者也易其至廣而无不包至大而无不有
者乎是故言乎遠而有所不達非廣大也易則
隨處充滿而无遠弗屆夫孰得而禦之言乎近
而或有所遺非廣大也易則隨在各足而小大
有定不亦靜而正乎又自夫天地之間言之體
物或遺非廣大也吾見察於上下莫非陰陽之
punctuated:
夫乾，其靜也專，其動也直，是以大生焉。夫坤，其靜也翕，其動也闢，是以廣生焉。

高士楠

同考試官教諭王批：說易廣大處，不易見得。
同考試官教諭劉批：長題能收拾。
同考試官教諭徐批：模寫造化，深見易理。
考試官教諭劉批：辭順理足。
考試官教授林批：純雅。

大傳詳易理之廣大，必推而本諸乾坤焉。夫易，冒天下之道者也。乾坤動靜之間，而廣大見之，易其性命之書矣乎？大傳之意若謂：易者，理之會也；乾坤者，理之迹也。人以易爲卜筮之書，非知易者也。易其至廣而无不包，至大而无不有者乎？是故言乎遠而有所不達，非廣大也；易則隨處充滿，而无遠弗屆，夫孰得而禦之？言乎近而或有所遺，非廣大也；易則隨在各足，而小大有定，不亦靜而正乎？又自夫天地之間言之，體物或遺，非廣大也。吾見察於上下，莫非陰陽之
translation_en:
… Qian, in stillness, is concentrated; in movement, it is direct. Hence greatness arises. Kun, in stillness, draws together; in movement, it opens out. Hence breadth arises.

Gao Shinan

Associate Examiner, Instructor Wang, comments: “In explaining the breadth and greatness of the Changes, he brings out what is not easily discerned.”
Associate Examiner, Instructor Liu, comments: “He manages to bring this long topic together.”
Associate Examiner, Instructor Xu, comments: “His portrayal of the creative transformations of nature reveals a profound understanding of the principles of the Changes.”
Examiner, Instructor Liu, comments: “The language flows smoothly, and the reasoning is ample.”
Examiner, Instructor Lin, comments: “Pure and elegant.”

In expounding the breadth and greatness of the principles of the Book of Changes, the Great Commentary necessarily traces them back to their foundation in Qian and Kun. The Changes encompasses the Way of all under Heaven. Its breadth and greatness appear in the movement and stillness of Qian and Kun. Is not the Changes, then, a book of human nature and destiny? The Great Commentary seems to mean that the Changes is where principles converge, while Qian and Kun are the visible traces of those principles. Those who regard the Changes as a book of divination by tortoise shell and milfoil do not understand it. Is it not so supremely broad that it embraces everything, and so supremely great that it contains everything?

Thus, speaking of what is distant, if there were anything it could not reach, it would not possess breadth and greatness. But the Changes fills every place, reaching even the most distant: what could possibly obstruct it? Speaking of what is near, if anything were left out, it would not possess breadth and greatness. But the Changes is complete wherever it is, with small and great each having its determined place: is this not stillness and correctness? Again, speaking of what lies between Heaven and Earth, if it failed to embody any thing, it would not possess breadth and greatness. I see, upon examining above and below, nothing but yin and yang’s …

title: 嘉靖十九年廣東鄉試錄
text:
流行塞乎天地无非變化之妙用兼體不累其
至矣乎然易之所以廣大者何哉觀乾坤則知
易矣夫乾以生物爲心自其靜而別於坤誠之
所復專而一也及其動而與坤交焉推行不息
普天下而有莫禦之機是其周遍之體蓋實而
无所不統矣大不於是而生乎乾之大卽易之
大焉耳夫坤以成物爲心自其靜而別於乾機
之所入翕而聚也及其動而與乾交焉充周不
窮合群動而有難名之化是其含弘之量蓋虛
===
而无所不容矣廣不於是而生乎坤之廣卽易
之廣焉耳此易書所以爲至而聖人統天地之
心者以此學者苟不求之乾坤於心之動靜曷
足以知之哉大抵易書未作易在造化易書旣
作造化在易故天地之大事物之微无不出於
陰陽之變聖人亦因而模寫之而已後世洞極
有書潛虛有圖欲以擬易牽合附會自然之理
益晦焉無惑乎天下以卜筮而小吾易也
書
punctuated:
流行，塞乎天地，无非變化之妙用，兼體不累，其至矣乎！然易之所以廣大者何哉？觀乾坤則知易矣。夫乾以生物爲心，自其靜而別於坤，誠之所復，專而一也；及其動而與坤交焉，推行不息，普天下而有莫禦之機，是其周遍之體，蓋實而无所不統矣。大不於是而生乎？乾之大，卽易之大焉耳。夫坤以成物爲心，自其靜而別於乾，機之所入，翕而聚也；及其動而與乾交焉，充周不窮，合群動而有難名之化，是其含弘之量，蓋虛而无所不容矣。廣不於是而生乎？坤之廣，卽易之廣焉耳。此易書所以爲至，而聖人統天地之心者以此。學者苟不求之乾坤於心之動靜，曷足以知之哉？大抵易書未作，易在造化；易書旣作，造化在易。故天地之大，事物之微，无不出於陰陽之變，聖人亦因而模寫之而已。後世《洞極》有書，《潛虛》有圖，欲以擬易，牽合附會，自然之理益晦焉。無惑乎天下以卜筮而小吾易也！

書
translation_en:
…flowing and circulating, filling Heaven and Earth: all is the wondrous operation of change and transformation. It embodies both without encumbrance—is this not perfection? Yet why is the Changes so broad and great? By observing Qian and Kun, one understands the Changes. Qian takes the generation of things as its heart. In its stillness, distinct from Kun, it is where sincerity returns, concentrated and unified. When it moves and joins with Kun, it advances without ceasing, extending throughout the world with an impetus that nothing can resist. Its all-pervading substance is thus full, leaving nothing outside its governance. Does not greatness arise from this? The greatness of Qian is simply the greatness of the Changes. Kun takes the completion of things as its heart. In its stillness, distinct from Qian, it is where the incipient impulse enters, drawn together and gathered in. When it moves and joins with Qian, it fills all space inexhaustibly, bringing all movements together in transformations difficult to name. Its capacious, encompassing capacity is thus empty, leaving nothing it cannot accommodate. Does not breadth arise from this? The breadth of Kun is simply the breadth of the Changes. This is why the book of Changes is supreme, and through this the sage comprehends the heart of Heaven and Earth. Unless students seek Qian and Kun in the movement and stillness of their own hearts, how can they adequately understand it? Broadly speaking, before the book of Changes was composed, the Changes resided in the workings of creation; once the book was composed, the workings of creation resided in the Changes. Thus, from the immensity of Heaven and Earth to the minutiae of affairs and things, nothing fails to issue from the transformations of yin and yang. The sage merely followed these and represented them. In later ages, there was the book Penetrating the Ultimate (Dongji), and there were diagrams in Fathoming the Void (Qianxu). Seeking to emulate the Changes, they forced correspondences and contrived connections, further obscuring the principles of what is naturally so. No wonder the world belittles our Changes as a work of divination!

title: 嘉靖十九年廣東鄉試錄
text:
安汝止惟幾惟康
林繼習
同考試官教諭蕭批以惟幾惟康為安汝止之實良是
考試官教諭劉批理明詞暢
考試官教授林批純正
事適本原之善而致謹於發用之間大臣告君
之脩己也蓋君心主天下之善而審之於為則
得之矣聖禹以此箴帝舜之謹位也有以哉想
其意豈不曰人君居天位而致治安者在乎事
===
為之善而事之善非在事也蓋吾之一心萬善
咸備事之所取無窮而吾之付之也各因其則
若有所定於中而其不可遷者是之謂止其止
也惟懼夫欲之為奪者矣帝也日觀萬化其必
以道心為主而帝德昭然其廣運使凡動靜云
為之發莫不各取其固有於吾道心而止焉如
天之運而日月星辰各得其麗也日臨萬幾其
必守中心無為而淵衷穆然其靜定使凡事事
物物之來莫不各還其本善於吾中心而安焉
punctuated:
安汝止，惟幾惟康。
林繼習
同考試官教諭蕭批：以惟幾惟康為安汝止之實，良是。
考試官教諭劉批：理明詞暢。
考試官教授林批：純正。
事適本原之善，而致謹於發用之間，大臣告君之脩己也。蓋君心主天下之善，而審之於為，則得之矣。聖禹以此箴帝舜之謹位也，有以哉！想其意，豈不曰：「人君居天位而致治安者，在乎事為之善。而事之善，非在事也。蓋吾之一心，萬善咸備；事之所取無窮，而吾之付之也，各因其則。若有所定於中，而其不可遷者，是之謂止。其止也，惟懼夫欲之為奪者矣。帝也日觀萬化，其必以道心為主，而帝德昭然其廣運，使凡動靜云為之發，莫不各取其固有於吾道心而止焉，如天之運而日月星辰各得其麗也。日臨萬幾，其必守中心無為，而淵衷穆然其靜定，使凡事事物物之來，莫不各還其本善於吾中心而安焉，
translation_en:
“Be secure in where you rest; attend to the beginnings of things and to peace.”
Lin Jixi (林繼習)
Associate Examiner Xiao, Instructor, comments: “He takes attending to beginnings and to peace as the substance of being secure in where one rests. This is indeed correct.”
Examiner Liu, Instructor, comments: “Clear reasoning and fluent expression.”
Examiner Lin, Professor, comments: “Pure and orthodox.”
To make affairs accord with goodness at its source, and to exercise care as that goodness comes into operation: this is a great minister’s counsel to his ruler on cultivating himself. The ruler’s mind presides over all goodness under Heaven; by examining it carefully in his actions, he realizes it. The sage Yu had good reason to use these words to admonish Emperor Shun to exercise care in occupying his position! If we imagine his meaning, was he not saying:
“A ruler occupies Heaven’s seat and brings about orderly and peaceful government through goodness in his undertakings. Yet the goodness of affairs does not reside in the affairs themselves. Within this single mind of mine, all forms of goodness are complete. What affairs draw upon is inexhaustible, and what I impart to each accords with its proper rule. There is, as it were, something settled within that cannot be shifted: this is what is meant by a resting place. In resting there, one fears only that desires may wrest it away.
“Your Majesty daily observes the myriad transformations. You must take the mind of the Way as your master, so that your imperial virtue shines forth in its far-reaching operation. Thus, whenever activity or stillness, speech or action issues forth, each draws upon what is inherently present in your mind of the Way and rests there, just as, in Heaven’s revolutions, the sun, moon, and stars each find their proper place. Daily you preside over the myriad incipient affairs. You must preserve nonaction within your mind, so that your profound inner being remains serene, still, and settled. Thus, as each affair and thing presents itself, each returns to its original goodness within your mind and rests securely there …

title: 嘉靖十九年廣東鄉試錄
text:
如地之容而山川人物各奠其居也是之謂安
汝止然所以能使之安者果何如哉蓋事之欲
爲而發動所由謂之幾幾分善惡在毫釐之間
惟己所獨知者矣帝於此必致審其念慮之發
眞所以昭德致理也而罔有飾僞之私則從而
發之如其未然則禦寇之剛不可不厲也事之
旣爲而適當其理謂之康康成於幾則微者以
著理無所容其僞矣帝於此又必致省於事爲
之迹果足以達善宣猷也而匪爲違道之行則
===
從而安之如其未然則改圖之功所不容已也
夫審幾以達外則察之精而其善爲益固如此而事有
以觀內則守之一而其善爲益固如此而事有
不得其所止者哉事得其止則治化益隆天位
可保於無窮矣帝其可不念哉抑聖禹幾康之
說是卽精一之旨舜所受之堯者厥後舜之禪
禹其所命精一之言亦卽幾康之意三聖相授
共守一道於此可見而幾之一字尤虞廷之所
致謹焉者故皐陶陳謨有曰一日二日萬幾舜
punctuated:
如地之容，而山川人物各奠其居也。是之謂安汝止。然所以能使之安者，果何如哉？蓋事之欲爲，而發動所由，謂之幾。幾分善惡，在毫釐之間，惟己所獨知者矣。帝於此必致審其念慮之發，眞所以昭德致理也，而罔有飾僞之私，則從而發之；如其未然，則禦寇之剛不可不厲也。事之旣爲，而適當其理，謂之康。康成於幾，則微者以著，理無所容其僞矣。帝於此又必致省於事爲之迹，果足以達善宣猷也，而匪爲違道之行，則從而安之；如其未然，則改圖之功所不容已也。
夫審幾以達外，則察之精，而其善爲益固如此，而事有以觀內，則守之一，而其善爲益固如此，而事有不得其所止者哉？事得其止，則治化益隆，天位可保於無窮矣。帝其可不念哉？抑聖禹幾康之說，是卽精一之旨，舜所受之堯者。厥後舜之禪禹，其所命精一之言，亦卽幾康之意。三聖相授，共守一道，於此可見。而幾之一字，尤虞廷之所致謹焉者。故皐陶陳謨有曰：「一日二日萬幾。」舜
translation_en:
…like the earth’s capacity to contain all things, whereby mountains, rivers, people, and creatures each find a settled dwelling. This is what is meant by “rest securely in your proper stopping place.” Yet how, precisely, can one make this repose secure? When an undertaking is about to be carried out, the incipient impulse from which its movement proceeds is called ji. At this incipient stage, good and evil diverge by the slightest degree, perceptible only to oneself. Here the emperor must scrutinize the emergence of his thoughts with the utmost care. If they truly serve to make virtue manifest and bring about good government, with no selfish impulse toward pretence or deception, he should give them expression. If they do not, he must exert the firmness with which one repels an invader. When an undertaking has been carried out and accords exactly with its proper principle, this is called kang, a state of settled well-being. Such well-being takes shape from incipient impulses: what was subtle becomes manifest, and principle leaves no room for falsity. Here the emperor must also examine most carefully the visible results of his actions. If they truly suffice to extend goodness and give effect to worthy plans, and constitute no conduct contrary to the Way, he should rest securely in them. If they do not, the work of revising his plans must not cease.
By scrutinizing incipient impulses so as to extend this understanding to outward affairs, one’s discernment becomes refined, and one’s goodness is thereby made increasingly firm. Affairs then provide a means of examining what lies within [?]; one’s adherence becomes single-minded, and one’s goodness is thereby made increasingly firm. With things thus, could any affair fail to attain its proper stopping place? When affairs attain their proper stopping places, government and moral transformation flourish ever more greatly, and the throne bestowed by Heaven can be preserved without end. Can the emperor fail to give thought to this? Moreover, the sage Yu’s teaching concerning incipient impulses and settled well-being is precisely the purport of refinement and single-mindedness, which Shun received from Yao. Later, when Shun abdicated in favor of Yu, his injunction concerning refinement and single-mindedness likewise conveyed the meaning of incipient impulses and settled well-being. Here we can see that the three sages transmitted their teaching to one another and together upheld a single Way. The single word ji, “incipient impulses,” was especially an object of the utmost vigilance at Shun’s court. Thus Gao Yao, in presenting his counsels, said: “In a single day or two, there are ten thousand incipient impulses.” Shun…

title: 嘉靖十九年廣東鄉試錄
text:
之作歌亦曰勅天之命惟時惟幾蓋天下之治
忽天人之去留誠於此係焉聖君賢臣所以兢
業而不敢忽而其警戒之言猶不忘於盛治之
時有由然也是故觀其道之同可以知往聖之
心學會其幾之審可以開萬世之太平
黍稷非馨明德惟馨
蕭來鳳
同考試官教諭蕭批發出周公之意無遺
考試官教諭劉批明整
考試官教授林批簡古
===
賢王舉聖訓著格神之本以命大臣也蓋至治
馨香則神之所格者誠不在於黍稷矣此周公
精微之訓而成王述之以告君陳也且昔周公
之意若曰祀以感神為極而治以明德為本有
其德則神易於感矣今夫君子脩明禋以事天
萃精神以假廟粢盛旣具於靜嘉則黍稷必列
於昭薦當是時也對越者無言奏假而感神明
之來享駿奔者顒若祼將而接靈貺之若通孰
punctuated:
之作歌亦曰：「勅天之命，惟時惟幾。」蓋天下之治忽、天人之去留，誠於此係焉。聖君賢臣所以兢業而不敢忽，而其警戒之言猶不忘於盛治之時，有由然也。是故觀其道之同，可以知往聖之心學；會其幾之審，可以開萬世之太平。

黍稷非馨，明德惟馨。
蕭來鳳
同考試官教諭蕭批：發出周公之意無遺。
考試官教諭劉批：明整。
考試官教授林批：簡古。

賢王舉聖訓，著格神之本，以命大臣也。蓋至治馨香，則神之所格者，誠不在於黍稷矣。此周公精微之訓，而成王述之以告君陳也。且昔周公之意若曰：「祀以感神為極，而治以明德為本。有其德，則神易於感矣。」今夫君子脩明禋以事天，萃精神以假廟，粢盛旣具於靜嘉，則黍稷必列於昭薦。當是時也，對越者無言，奏假而感神明之來享；駿奔者顒若，祼將而接靈貺之若通。孰
translation_en:
…in composing his song, he also said: “Attend reverently to Heaven’s mandate; attend to the times and to the first stirrings of change.” For order or disorder throughout the realm, and whether Heaven and the people withdraw their support or remain, truly depend upon this. There is good reason why sage rulers and worthy ministers remain vigilant and dare not be negligent, and why they do not forget words of admonition even in times of flourishing government. Thus, by observing the unity of their Way, one can understand the learning of the mind practiced by the sages of old; by comprehending their discerning attention to the first stirrings of change, one can establish peace for myriad generations.

“It is not the millet that is fragrant; it is luminous virtue that is fragrant.”
Xiao Laifeng 蕭來鳳
Associate Examiner Xiao, Instructor, comments: “Brings out the Duke of Zhou’s meaning, leaving nothing unexpressed.”
Examiner Liu, Instructor, comments: “Clear and orderly.”
Examiner Lin, Professor, comments: “Concise and antique in style.”

The worthy king cited a sage’s teaching to make clear the foundation for drawing the spirits near, thereby instructing his great minister. For it is consummate government that gives forth fragrance; what draws the spirits near truly does not lie in the millet. This was the Duke of Zhou’s subtle and profound teaching, which King Cheng recounted in admonishing Jun Chen. The Duke of Zhou’s meaning in former times was as if to say: “Sacrifice has as its ultimate aim moving the spirits, while government has luminous virtue as its foundation. Possess that virtue, and the spirits are readily moved.” Now, when the gentleman performs pure sacrifices to serve Heaven and concentrates his spiritual energies to approach the ancestral temple, once the grain offerings have been prepared in purity and excellence, the millet must be arrayed in splendid presentation. At that moment, those standing reverently before the spirits are wordless: they advance and approach, moving the divine powers to come and partake. title: 嘉靖十九年廣東鄉試錄
text:
不以爲黍稷之馨而致然也殊不知簋實特所
以羞神而祀有不求於備物略儀文之末節求
苾芬之實體夫豈專在於黍稷之具而已哉誠
以至治成於有本而康乂之休莫非至德之薰
蒸大化神於不顯而太和之美莫非明德之融
液敷聞在下則昭升于上上帝時歆其鬯達固
不待黍稷之陳矣而况禮行於郊社有不降監
者乎精華旁達則馨香發聞百神胥悅其和氣
固出於黍稷之外矣而况祀事之孔明有不昭
===
格者乎周公之訓如此則知不能明德以治民
者不可以事神君陳之尹東郊有神民之寄可
不懋昭周公之訓以自明其德而化訓殷民以
求無斁於神乎抑殷民爲梗周公誕保之而東
郊之尹繼以君陳將舉周公之政必師周公之
德而後可故成王命君陳首以周公之訓爲言
欲其近法而不違襲德而不貳庶漸濡相繼頑
民懷服無異於周公時也下文式時猷訓敬典
在德之言成王復爲君陳丁寧之卒之殷民式
punctuated: 不以爲黍稷之馨而致然也？殊不知簋實特所以羞神，而祀有不求於備物。略儀文之末節，求苾芬之實體，夫豈專在於黍稷之具而已哉？誠以至治成於有本，而康乂之休，莫非至德之薰蒸；大化神於不顯，而太和之美，莫非明德之融液。敷聞在下，則昭升于上，上帝時歆，其鬯達固不待黍稷之陳矣，而况禮行於郊社，有不降監者乎？精華旁達，則馨香發聞，百神胥悅，其和氣固出於黍稷之外矣，而况祀事之孔明，有不昭格者乎？周公之訓如此，則知不能明德以治民者，不可以事神。君陳之尹東郊，有神民之寄，可不懋昭周公之訓，以自明其德，而化訓殷民，以求無斁於神乎？抑殷民爲梗，周公誕保之，而東郊之尹繼以君陳。將舉周公之政，必師周公之德而後可。故成王命君陳，首以周公之訓爲言，欲其近法而不違，襲德而不貳，庶漸濡相繼，頑民懷服，無異於周公時也。下文「式時猷訓」「敬典在德」之言，成王復爲君陳丁寧之。卒之殷民式
translation_en:
… would not attribute this to the fragrance of the sacrificial millet? Yet they fail to understand that the contents of the ritual vessels merely serve as offerings to the spirits, and that sacrifice involves something beyond the completeness of its offerings. Setting aside the minor details of ceremonial forms and seeking the true substance of that fragrance, how could it consist solely in the provision of millet? Indeed, perfect government rests upon a foundation: the blessings of peace and order all arise from the pervasive influence of consummate virtue. Great transformation works wondrously in the unseen: the beauty of supreme harmony all arises from the permeating influence of luminous virtue. As its renown spreads below, it rises resplendently above, and the Lord on High delights in it. Its fragrance surely reaches him without waiting for the millet to be set out. How much more, then, when rites are performed at the suburban altar and the altar of soil: could he fail to descend and behold them? As its pure essence spreads in every direction, its fragrance becomes manifest, and the hundred spirits all rejoice. Its harmonious influence surely extends beyond the millet. How much more, then, when the sacrificial service is conducted with great brilliance: could the spirits fail to come in manifest presence?

Such was the teaching of the Duke of Zhou. From it we know that anyone unable to make virtue luminous in governing the people cannot serve the spirits. Jun Chen, as administrator of the eastern suburbs, was entrusted with responsibility for both spirits and people. Could he fail diligently to make manifest the Duke of Zhou’s teaching, thereby illuminating his own virtue and transforming and instructing the people of Yin, so that the spirits would never tire of him?

Moreover, when the people of Yin were refractory, the Duke of Zhou gave them ample protection; Jun Chen then succeeded him as administrator of the eastern suburbs. To carry forward the Duke of Zhou’s government, he first had to take the Duke’s virtue as his model. Thus, in charging Jun Chen, King Cheng began by invoking the Duke of Zhou’s teaching. He wished Jun Chen to follow this recent model without departing from it and to inherit its virtue without wavering, so that the gradual influence of instruction might continue uninterrupted and the obstinate people might become devoted and submissive, just as in the Duke of Zhou’s time. In the words that follow—“Follow these counsels and teachings” and “Reverence for the constant norms lies in virtue”—King Cheng again earnestly admonished Jun Chen. title: 嘉靖十九年廣東鄉試錄
text:
化世變風移君陳和中之治端有力焉而成王
之因時制宜命德命治憂勤馴擾之心不少置
焉嗚呼繼體守成之君其有賢於成王哉
詩
物其多矣維其嘉矣物其旨矣維其偕矣
物其有矣維其時矣
蒙詔
同考試官教諭甘批辭不費而事理詳盡
同考試官教諭陳批優賓之情宛然可見
===
考試官教諭劉批才思清妙
考試官教授林批精潔
觀主人優賓之意自夫物之曲全見之矣夫燕
飲之禮以備物為尚也主人燕賓而能曲全焉
是不可以觀敬乎哉此燕饗通用之樂歌以為
燕也者所以昭嘉會之禮洽賓主之情者也儀
不及物是曰不享然享非多儀無乃太簡乎是
故物有以多為貴者多而不嘉雖多奚以為也
今君子有酒多且旨吾見嘉寓於多焉尊罍皆
punctuated:
化，世變風移，君陳和中之治端有力焉。而成王之因時制宜，命德命治，憂勤馴擾之心不少置焉。嗚呼！繼體守成之君，其有賢於成王哉？

觀主人優賓之意，自夫物之曲全見之矣。夫燕飲之禮，以備物為尚也。主人燕賓而能曲全焉，是不可以觀敬乎哉？此燕饗通用之樂歌，以為燕也者，所以昭嘉會之禮、洽賓主之情者也。儀不及物，是曰不享。然享非多儀，無乃太簡乎？是故物有以多為貴者，多而不嘉，雖多奚以為也？今君子有酒，多且旨，吾見嘉寓於多焉。尊罍皆

Among rulers who inherited the throne and preserved their predecessors’ achievements, was there any worthier than King Cheng?
